entries.clue: State "Mate almost president!" (6)

indicatorNotes.almost: Almost stops just short of the whole thing, so the word beside it arrives without its final letter.

blocks.note: MA is the two-letter postal code for Massachusetts, one of the United States
a crony is a mate, and the word is taken one letter short of its end

annotation.surface: One friend hailing another as very nearly head of state.
annotation.walkthrough: State looks like the grand noun the exclamation is about and is a US postal abbreviation. The mate the wordplay wants is a crony, a word the clue never prints.
annotation.definitionFit: Emmanuel Macron has been President of France since 2017, so the clue names the office and expects the man who holds it.

entries.clue: Mediocre, interfering head of education is replaced by one (8)

indicatorNotes.head of: The head of a word is its front, so the letter wanted is the one it begins with.
indicatorNotes.is replaced by: One thing replaced by another leaves altogether, and the second stands in the gap it left.

blocks.note: meddling is interfering in what is none of your business
the letter the word starts with, taken as instructed
i is the Roman numeral for one

annotation.surface: A meddlesome education chief pushed out and a single replacement put in.
annotation.walkthrough: Head of education reads as the person running the schools, and only the letter at the front of the word is wanted. One arrives as the Roman numeral, a single letter stepping into a single letter's place.
annotation.definitionFit: Something middling is halfway up the scale and goes no further, which is the shrug that mediocre gives.

entries.clue: Almost the last conduit for our shit currency (5)

annotation.definition: Almost the last conduit for our shit

blocks.clueFragment: Almost the last conduit for our shit
blocks.note: the long stretch of bowel that waste passes through on its way out, with only the rectum after it
the money of Costa Rica and El Salvador, named after Columbus in Spanish

annotation.surface: The last remaining channel through which our worthless money still moves.
annotation.walkthrough: The sentence reads as one phrase about money, but the seam falls before currency. The Central American coin takes an accent the grid cannot show, which is how the setter gets two senses out of five letters.
annotation.definitionFit: The colon is the last stretch of bowel before the rectum, hence almost last; the colón is the currency of Costa Rica and El Salvador.

entries.clue: Sun rogue held in honour – cover up! (7)

indicatorNotes.held in: What is held in something sits inside it, so the letters named before go within the ones named after.

blocks.note: the OBE, the Order of the British Empire, is the honour handed out in the King's list twice a year
s is the short form of sun in weather tables and almanacs
a cur is a mongrel dog, and a man called one is a rogue

annotation.surface: A scoundrel at the Sun newspaper being held in high honour.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash does all the separating: everything before it is wordplay. Cur for a man is an old insult that survives mainly in crosswords, and the medal named here is the one every British honours list hands out.
annotation.definitionFit: To obscure something is to cover it up, putting a view or a fact out of sight rather than tidying it away.

entries.clue: Be a she, artfully grabbing Jack for starters (7)

indicatorNotes.artfully: Artful means done by cunning rather than straight, and letters handled that way do not stay in the order given.
indicatorNotes.grabbing: To grab a thing is to take hold of it and keep it, so the letter named lands inside.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
j = jack, the card between the ten and the queen

annotation.surface: Advice to impersonate a woman, cleverly seizing Jack before anything else.
annotation.walkthrough: For starters reads as first of all and is the definition. Bhajees are the deep-fried onion fritters at the top of an Indian menu, which is what puts them in that course.
annotation.definitionFit: A bhajee is the onion fritter that opens an Indian meal, so the plural names a menu course rather than a synonym.

entries.clue: (& 6dn.) It's bad for a person's reputation, showing chopper at office (7)

annotation.definition: It's bad for a person's reputation
annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a sentence about the answer rather than a word for it: the it is the thing being defined, named by the damage it does.

blocks.note: a hatchet is the short-handled chopper for splitting kindling
the office a person holds is their job, the post they occupy

annotation.surface: A helicopter parked outside the office, doing nobody's good name any favours.
annotation.walkthrough: Chopper is the helicopter in the picture and the small axe in the wordplay. The answer runs on into 6 down, which is where the second piece goes.
annotation.definitionFit: A hatchet job is a review or a briefing written to wreck somebody's standing, so the clue defines it by the harm it is meant to do.

entries.clue: see 5dn.
All together: "Incredible – noble Conservative!" (2,4)

indicatorNotes.Incredible: What is incredible cannot be taken as it stands, and the letters beside it are not to be taken as they stand either.

blocks.note: the five letters of the word redealt
c = Conservative, the party's letter on a ballot paper

annotation.surface: A crowd shouting its admiration for a Tory aristocrat.
annotation.walkthrough: The phrase is French taken whole: a council that resigns this way goes in one lump, nobody staying behind. The quotation marks are surface dressing and ask for nothing to be said aloud.
annotation.definitionFit: To act en bloc is to act as one undivided body, everybody moving at the same moment, which is what all together says.

entries.clue: (&16dn/23dn.) Have a snog, then do it again, side by side (4)

blocks.note: to neck is to kiss and cuddle at length
then joins one thing to the next, which is the job and does
the same instruction served a second time, for the same four letters

annotation.surface: Instructions for a snog and an immediate encore.
annotation.walkthrough: Snogging is British for a long kiss, and the verb behind it is the piece repeated here. The phrase comes from racing, where two horses run level with their necks abreast.
annotation.definitionFit: Two runners neck and neck are drawn level with each other, from horses finishing with necks abreast, so side by side is meant literally.

entries.clue: One on benefit going to Cologne? Immature (10)

blocks.note: a is the article standing for one of a thing
somebody on benefit is on the dole, Britain's long-standing word for unemployment payments
cologne is a light scent, and the question mark admits it is one kind among many

annotation.surface: A benefit claimant heading off to the Rhineland for a holiday.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital letter makes Cologne the German city while the wordplay wants the perfume named after it. Immature is the definition and an adjective, so the answer is used as one.
annotation.definitionFit: An adolescent is still growing into an adult, which is what immature says of a person rather than of fruit.

entries.clue: Love second-rate, familiar old president (4)

blocks.note: b is the second grade, the mark one below an a
Abe is the familiar form of Abraham Lincoln's name

annotation.surface: Being fond of a mediocre and all too familiar ex-president.
annotation.walkthrough: Love is the address rather than the feeling: it is what one person calls another in a shop queue. Abraham Lincoln is Abe to Americans, which is the familiarity the clue asks for.
annotation.definitionFit: Babe is what you call a sweetheart, the same endearment that love is in everyday British speech.

entries.clue: Trump's on-off buddy, lone rogue, odorous thing (4,4)

indicatorNotes.rogue: A rogue element is one that has gone out of line, and the letters beside it have gone out of theirs.

blocks.note: the four letters of the word redealt
musk is the heavy animal scent perfumers use

annotation.surface: A description of Trump's unreliable friend as a solitary chancer who smells.
annotation.walkthrough: Lone rogue reads as a character sketch and is an instruction about four letters. The second half wants the perfumer's word, which happens to be spelt like a surname.
annotation.definitionFit: Elon Musk bankrolled Trump's 2024 campaign, ran his cost-cutting drive and then fell out with him in public, which is the on-off the clue notes.

entries.clue: Biscuit at first neatly inserted in bum by bishop (6)

indicatorNotes.at first: At first points at the front of the word beside it, so only its opening letter is taken.
indicatorNotes.inserted in: To insert a thing in something is to push it into the middle, so the letter goes within.

blocks.note: a hobo is a bum, the American tramp riding the freight trains
the letter the word starts with, taken as instructed
b is the bishop on a chess scoresheet

annotation.surface: A bishop carefully posting a biscuit where no biscuit should go.
annotation.walkthrough: Bum is the American tramp, not the British backside the surface is grinning at. To hobnob, in the other sense of the word, is to mix socially with people grander than you.
annotation.definitionFit: A Hobnob is the oat-and-syrup biscuit McVitie's have sold in Britain since 1985, so biscuit is the plain category it sits in.

entries.clue: Disgraced leader's book: Alternative Lives (5)

blocks.note: b is the standard short form of book
or is the word that sets one thing against another as the alternative
he lives and he is come to the same thing in the third person

annotation.surface: A fallen leader's memoir published under the title Alternative Lives.
annotation.walkthrough: Alternative Lives reads as the title printed on the cover, and both words are doing separate jobs underneath. The leader is the prime minister forced out in 2022 over parties held in Downing Street during lockdown.
annotation.definitionFit: Boris Johnson resigned as prime minister in disgrace in 2022, and Private Eye's readers know him by the first name alone.

entries.clue: Be facilitating, acquiescent  – but not in the morning (6)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition puts the verb in the continuous where the answer is the bare form, so that the sentence can carry on into the surface.

indicatorNotes.but not: But not cancels whatever is named after it, so those letters never reach the grid.

blocks.note: somebody amenable is acquiescent, willing to go along with whatever is proposed
am is the morning half of the clock, and it is the pair of letters taken away

annotation.surface: Somebody helpful and agreeable, though never before lunch.
annotation.walkthrough: In the morning reads as a remark about when the agreeable person is at their worst and is two letters lifted off the front. Am is the ante meridiem of any clock face.
annotation.definitionFit: To enable something is to make it possible, clearing the way for it rather than doing the thing yourself, which is what facilitating means.

entries.clue: The old form of punishment: coming before terribly rich bastard (5)

indicatorNotes.coming before: Coming before puts the piece it governs in front of the rest, which fixes where the single letter lands.
indicatorNotes.terribly: Something done terribly is done badly, and letters handled badly do not come out in the order they went in.

blocks.note: b is the printable first letter of the insult
the four letters of the word redealt

annotation.surface: An old sentence handed down before a fabulously rich swine.
annotation.walkthrough: The punishment is a bundle of twigs used to flog offenders, abolished in British courts in 1948 and on the Isle of Man only in 1976. Coming before looks like a court appearance and is telling you where one letter goes.
annotation.definitionFit: The birch is the bundle of twigs offenders were once flogged with, and to be given the birch is to be given that punishment.

entries.clue: Bloomer showing behind almost (5)

indicatorNotes.almost: Almost falls just short, so the word beside it arrives without its final letter.

blocks.note: the sailor's word for whatever lies to the rear of a ship, which gives up its final letter here

annotation.surface: An embarrassing mistake very nearly on show round the back.
annotation.walkthrough: Bloomer is the blunder in the surface and a plant in the definition. Behind is meant nautically here, which is the only reading that gives a word to cut short.
annotation.definitionFit: An aster is the daisy-like garden flower that blooms in autumn, so bloomer is meant in its plain sense: a thing that blooms.

entries.clue: see 8dn.
"Nurse, I've cocked up just about everything!" (8)

indicatorNotes.cocked up: To cock something up is to make a mess of it, and a word made a mess of does not keep its letters in place.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: A patient on the ward confessing to the nurse that he has ruined everything.
annotation.walkthrough: Just about everything reads as the patient's hopeless exaggeration and is a fair description of all existence. The quotation marks are surface only: nothing here is being sounded out.
annotation.definitionFit: The universe is everything there is, and just about concedes the slack between a loose phrase and literally all that exists.

entries.clue: Raging Republican wants an offer (5)

blocks.note: r = Republican on an American ballot paper
the article, which the charade takes as the letter a
a bid is the offer made in an auction room

annotation.surface: A furious Republican waiting for somebody to make him an offer.
annotation.walkthrough: Raging is the definition and an adjective, so the answer has to be one too. Republican looks like the man in the picture and gives up a single letter, the one beside his name on the ballot.
annotation.definitionFit: A rabid supporter rages past all reason, the word carried over from the disease that leaves animals frenzied.

entries.clue: Criminal gang leader interrupting internet address in pub (7)

indicatorNotes.leader: The leader of a word is the letter at its head, the one that goes in front.
indicatorNotes.interrupting: To interrupt something is to break into the middle of it, so the letter lands inside.
indicatorNotes.in: In puts whatever comes before it inside whatever comes after.

blocks.note: the bar is the pub, the room the drinking is done in
a URL is the uniform resource locator, the address typed into a browser
the letter the word starts with, taken as instructed

annotation.surface: A gang boss cutting in on somebody reading out a web address in the pub.
annotation.walkthrough: Criminal reads as the adjective describing the gang and is the definition, a noun. One insertion sits inside another, which is how three short pieces make seven letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A burglar is the criminal who breaks into buildings to steal, so the noun names one particular member of the class.

entries.clue: Bill might be given it by King Brian – fool goes to hospital (6)

annotation.definition: Bill might be given it by King Brian
annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a sentence in which the answer stands as it, named by who grants it rather than by any synonym.

blocks.note: an ass is a fool, the donkey's name turned into an insult
ENT is the ear, nose and throat department every hospital runs

annotation.surface: Bill getting something out of King Brian while a fool is carted off to hospital.
annotation.walkthrough: Private Eye has called Charles Brian for decades, so King Brian is the King himself and Bill is the one going through Parliament. Both wordplay pieces sit after the dash.
annotation.definitionFit: A Bill becomes law only once the monarch grants it royal assent, the formal agreement the Crown gives, which is the it the sentence hands over.

entries.clue: Very good name in Gaelic rum (7)

indicatorNotes.in: In places the letter it follows inside the letters it points at.
indicatorNotes.rum: Rum is the old British word for odd or peculiar, and letters called odd are not in their proper order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
n = name, the abbreviation printed on forms

annotation.surface: A rather fine name for a peculiar Gaelic rum.
annotation.walkthrough: Rum is the adjective, not the drink: in British usage a rum business is an odd one. Very good reads in the surface as approval of the name and is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: To call behaviour angelic is to call it very good, faultless in the way an angel is rather than merely obedient.

entries.clue: Spotted parking easily, being topless (6)

indicatorNotes.being topless: Something topless has lost whatever sat on top of it, and in a down entry that is the first letter.

blocks.note: p is the parking sign on every British street
simply means easily, and the word arrives without the letter on top

annotation.surface: Finding a parking space without trouble, and with nothing on above the waist.
annotation.walkthrough: Spotted is the trap: it offers itself as noticed and means covered in spots. Topless works vertically because this is a down entry, taking the letter at the head of the word.
annotation.definitionFit: A pimply face is covered in spots, which is what spotted says of skin rather than of a leopard.

entries.clue: Hesitate and only half do it with female (6)

indicatorNotes.only half: Only half keeps one of the two letters and throws the other away, and it is the front half that stays.

blocks.note: half of a two-letter word is one letter, the one at the front
the word taken exactly as it stands
her is the female pronoun

annotation.surface: Hanging back, then only half doing it with a woman.
annotation.walkthrough: Do it reads as a single euphemism and comes apart into two pieces, the first of them halved. Hesitate is the definition, a verb, so the answer is one.
annotation.definitionFit: To dither is to hover between choices without settling on any, which is hesitating stretched out over time.

entries.clue: Being squeezed by local inhabitant, say "no" (8)

indicatorNotes.Being squeezed by: To be squeezed by something is to be pressed inside it, so the short piece goes within the longer one.

blocks.note: a native is the inhabitant born in the place, the local
e.g. is Latin for for example, which is what say means when it offers an instance

annotation.surface: Somebody pinned in the grip of a local resident and managing only to refuse.
annotation.walkthrough: Say is the abbreviation, not a request to speak: e.g. means for example and so does say. The quoted no is the definition, and it is a noun.
annotation.definitionFit: A negative is the answer that refuses, the no a question gets, as in replying in the negative.

entries.clue: see 8dn.
Tears over stunner (5)

indicatorNotes.over: Something turned over comes out in a different arrangement from the one it went in with.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters

annotation.surface: Weeping over a great beauty.
annotation.walkthrough: Stunner offers itself as the good-looking woman and means the thing that stuns. In a down entry over usually flags a reversal, which is the false trail here.
annotation.definitionFit: A Taser drops whoever it hits with an electric shock, so stunner names it by exactly what it does.

entries.clue: Gob, ultimately famous, mine (4)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: Ultimately points at the end of the word beside it, so only its final letter is taken.

blocks.note: the last letter of the word, taken as instructed
a pit is a mine, the word the old British coalfields used

annotation.surface: Somebody's mouth, famous in the end, and the mine they came out of.
annotation.walkthrough: Mine is the noun, the colliery, not the possessive the sentence offers. Gob does double duty in British slang, naming the mouth and what comes out of it.
annotation.definitionFit: To gob is British slang for to spit, and a gob of phlegm is the spit itself, so the two words trade places freely.

entries.clue: Dope Cyclops introduced to race (3)

indicatorNotes.introduced to: To introduce a thing to something is to put it in, so the letter goes inside.

blocks.note: the TT is the Tourist Trophy, the motorcycle race run on Isle of Man roads
the setter writes himself in as I, the single eye he is named for

annotation.surface: A fool taking Cyclops along to the Isle of Man races.
annotation.walkthrough: Cyclops signs himself into his own wordplay, and the one-eyed giant is why the letter is I rather than anything else. The TT has been run on Manx roads since 1907.
annotation.definitionFit: Calling somebody a tit is calling them a fool in mild British slang, which is the register dope works in too.

entries.clue: Want unpredictable result? How dull! (10)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is the exclamation a dull thing draws rather than an adjective standing on its own, and the solver supplies the word behind the complaint.

indicatorNotes.unpredictable: What is unpredictable will not come out the way you expect, and neither will the letters beside it.

blocks.note: to want something is to lack it, the older sense of the verb
the six letters of the word redealt

annotation.surface: Somebody hoping for an unpredictable result and finding the whole idea tedious.
annotation.walkthrough: Want is the old sense, to lack, which crosswords keep alive long after ordinary speech let it go. The question mark marks the seam: everything before it is wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Something lacklustre has no shine to it, flat and spiritless, and draws exactly the complaint the clue makes.

entries.clue: Cyclops's rest disturbed – end of Jimmy Riddle (7)

indicatorNotes.disturbed: Something disturbed has been knocked out of the arrangement it was in, letters included.
indicatorNotes.end of: End of points at the final letter of the word that follows it.

blocks.note: the setter speaks as himself, so whatever belongs to Cyclops is my
the four letters of the word redealt
the last letter of the name, taken as instructed

annotation.surface: Cyclops's sleep broken, and the end of a Jimmy Riddle.
annotation.walkthrough: Jimmy Riddle is Cockney rhyming slang for a piddle, which is the joke in the surface; the wordplay wants only the last letter of the name. Riddle on its own is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Both words name something nobody has worked out yet, and a riddle in the loose sense is simply a mystery waiting to be solved.

entries.clue: Start hoarding carbon (like gold dust) (6)

indicatorNotes.hoarding: To hoard a thing is to keep it shut away inside, which is where the letter named next goes.

blocks.note: a start is a scare, the jump you give when something frightens you
c is carbon's symbol on the periodic table

annotation.surface: An instruction to begin stockpiling carbon because so little of it is about.
annotation.walkthrough: Start is the noun, the jolt of fright, not the verb the instruction seems to give. Like gold dust is the everyday British idiom for whatever has run short in the shops.
annotation.definitionFit: Anything in such short supply that people fight over it is said to be like gold dust, which is scarcity put as an idiom.
